background:
Philippians: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

Study notes · dates are approximate and scholars vary

At a glance

Philippians is Paul's letter of joy, written from prison to his most faithful church. It thanks them for a gift, encourages them to stand together, and points them to Christ's humility. Most date it to Paul's house arrest in Rome, AD 60–62.

QuestionTraditional viewNotes
AuthorPaul, with Timothy (1:1)Accepted by virtually all scholars as Paul's.
DateAbout AD 60–62Some scholars propose an imprisonment in Ephesus about AD 54–55.
Written fromPrison, probably in RomePaul mentions “the whole praetorian guard” (1:13) and “Caesar's household” (4:22).
RecipientsThe church at Philippi, with its bishops and deacons (1:1)The first church Paul founded in Europe, about AD 49–50 (Acts 16).
OccasionA gift brought by Epaphroditus (4:18)Epaphroditus fell gravely ill in Rome and recovered; Paul sends him home with this letter (2:25–30).
Key wordsJoy and rejoice, about 16 timesWritten by a man in chains facing a possible death sentence.

At the center of the letter is a hymn about Christ, who “emptied himself” and was then highly exalted (2:5–11), the pattern Paul wants the church to follow.

Paul's life and the writing of Philippians

Dates are approximate. Philippians is one of four “prison letters,” with Ephesians, Colossians and Philemon.

The time map

The shaded band marks AD 60–62, Paul's two years of house arrest. In AD 62 Nero's chief advisers were gone, and two years later came the fire and persecution.

Rome in AD 60–62: Paul in chains

Paul wrote while chained to a soldier, awaiting the emperor's verdict.

  • House arrest. Paul lived “in his own hired dwelling” with a soldier guarding him (Acts 28:16, 30), probably chained by the wrist. Visitors could come and go.
  • The Praetorian Guard. The emperor's elite guard, about 9,000 men, based in a great camp in Rome. Rotating guards heard Paul's message, so “my bonds became manifest in Christ throughout the whole praetorian guard” (1:13).
  • Caesar's household. Not the emperor's family, but the thousands of slaves and freedmen who ran the imperial palace and government. Some of them were believers (4:22).
  • Life or death. Paul did not know whether the verdict would mean release or execution (1:20–26). He expected to be released, and tradition says he was.
  • Nero's turn. In AD 62 Burrus died and Seneca retired, and Nero's rule grew harsher. In AD 64 he blamed Christians for the Great Fire.
  • Emperor worship. Emperors were hailed as “Lord” and “Savior.” Paul gives those titles to Jesus, before whom “every knee should bow” (2:10–11; 3:20).

From the center of Roman power, Paul writes that he has “learned, in whatsoever state I am, therein to be content” (4:11).

Philippi: a little Rome in Macedonia

Philippi was proud to be Roman, and Paul uses that pride to teach the church who they really are.

  • A battlefield city. In 42 BC Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius, Julius Caesar's assassins, on the plain at Philippi. Veterans were settled there afterward.
  • A Roman colony. After his victory at Actium (31 BC), Octavian (Augustus) refounded the city as a colony with more veterans. Its people were Roman citizens, governed by Roman law, with Latin as the official language.
  • On the Via Egnatia. The great Roman road from the Adriatic to Byzantium ran through the city's forum.
  • Citizenship. Philippians prized their Roman citizenship. Paul tells them, “our citizenship is in heaven” (3:20), and uses a word that means “live as citizens” (1:27).
  • The church. It began with Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, a slave girl set free from a spirit, and a Roman jailer (Acts 16). Women such as Euodia and Syntyche were leaders (4:2–3).
  • Generous partners. The Philippians supported Paul again and again, in Thessalonica, in Corinth and now in Rome (4:15–16; 2 Cor 11:9), though they were not rich.

Around the world in AD 60–62

While Paul sat chained in Rome, the empire was busy on many fronts.

RegionWhat was happening
BritainBoudica's revolt (AD 60–61). The queen of the Iceni burned London, Colchester and St Albans before being crushed.
RomeNero's early good years ended about AD 62. The Great Fire of AD 64 was followed by the first persecution of Christians.
JudeaTension grew; James the Lord's brother was killed in AD 62. The Jewish revolt broke out in AD 66.
Armenia and ParthiaA compromise peace in AD 63; Nero crowned the Parthian prince Tiridates king of Armenia in Rome in AD 66.
ItalyAn earthquake damaged Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 62, seventeen years before Vesuvius buried them.
ChinaThe Eastern Han dynasty under Emperor Ming; silk reached Rome along the trade routes.
IndiaThe Kushan Empire was forming in the northwest; tradition says Thomas preached in India.
The AmericasTeotihuacan was growing; the Moche and Nazca cultures flourished in Peru.

How the setting shapes the study

The pride of a Roman colony and the realities of Paul's imprisonment shed light on many verses.

PassageConnection to the times
Phil 1:13The Praetorian Guard was the emperor's own elite force.
Phil 1:27“Let your manner of life be worthy” translates a word meaning “live as citizens.”
Phil 2:6–11Emperors claimed divine honors; Jesus, truly in the form of God, “emptied himself” and took the form of a slave.
Phil 2:15“Lights in the world” in a city whose public life centered on emperor worship.
Phil 3:5–6Paul lists his credentials the way Romans listed their offices and honors on inscriptions.
Phil 3:20Philippi was a colony of Rome; the church is a colony of heaven, awaiting a Savior from there.
Phil 4:3“True yokefellow” may be a person's name, Syzygus; enrollment in a “book of life” echoes city citizen rolls.
Phil 4:18Paul describes their gift as “an odor of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable.”
Phil 4:22“Caesar's household” were the slaves and freedmen of the imperial service.

To a church proud of being Roman, Paul says their true homeland and their true Lord are in heaven.

Maps: then and now

Philippi and Rome were about 800 miles apart. Travelers took the Appian Way to Brundisium, crossed the Adriatic, and followed the Via Egnatia east, a journey of about a month.

Today Philippi's ruins lie about 10 miles inland from the port of Kavala in northern Greece. They include the forum, a theater and a crypt that tradition associates with Paul's prison.

items.text: Greeting, Thanksgiving and Prayer
Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all the saints in Christ Jesus that are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
I thank my God upon all my remembrance of you,
always in every supplication of mine on behalf of you all making my supplication with joy,
for your fellowship in furtherance of the gospel from the first day until now;
being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Jesus Christ:

even as it is right for me to be thus minded on behalf of you all, because I have you in my heart, inasmuch as, both in my bonds and in the defence and confirmation of the gospel, ye all are partakers with me of grace.
For God is my witness, how I long after you all in the tender mercies of Christ Jesus.
And this I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and all discernment;
so that ye may approve the things that are excellent; that ye may be sincere and void of offence unto the day of Christ;
being filled with the fruits of righteousness, which are through Jesus Christ, unto the glory and praise of God.
The Gospel Advances Through Paul's Chains
Now I would have you know, brethren, that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the progress of the gospel;
so that my bonds became manifest in Christ throughout the whole prætorian guard, and to all the rest;
and that most of the brethren in the Lord, being confident through my bonds, are more abundantly bold to speak the word of God without fear.
Some indeed preach Christ even of envy and strife; and some also of good will:
the one do it of love, knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel;
but the other proclaim Christ of faction, not sincerely, thinking to raise up affliction for me in my bonds.
What then? only that in every way, whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and therein I rejoice, yea, and will rejoice.
To Live Is Christ, to Die Is Gain
For I know that this shall turn out to my salvation, through your supplication and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ,

according to my earnest expectation and hope, that in nothing shall I be put to shame, but that with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether by life, or by death.
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
But if to live in the flesh,—if this shall bring fruit from my work, then what I shall choose I know not.
But I am in a strait betwixt the two, having the desire to depart and be with Christ; for it is very far better:
yet to abide in the flesh is more needful for your sake.
And having this confidence, I know that I shall abide, yea, and abide with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith;
that your glorying may abound in Christ Jesus in me through my presence with you again.

Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ: that, whether I come and see you or be absent, I may hear of your state, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one soul striving for the faith of the gospel;
and in nothing affrighted by the adversaries: which is for them an evident token of perdition, but of your salvation, and that from God;
because to you it hath been granted in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer in his behalf:
having the same conflict which ye saw in me, and now hear to be in me.

summary.title: CHAPTER 1 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul thanks God every time he remembers the Philippians, for their partnership in the gospel from the first day, and he is confident that “he who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Jesus Christ.” He prays that their love may abound more and more in knowledge and discernment.

He tells them that his imprisonment has actually advanced the gospel: the whole praetorian guard knows he is in chains for Christ, and other believers have grown bolder. Even those who preach out of rivalry are spreading Christ, and he rejoices. Facing possible death, he writes, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” He expects to remain for their progress, and urges them to live as worthy citizens of the gospel, standing firm together without fear.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: How does Paul interpret his imprisonment in verses 12–18, and what reasons does he give for rejoicing even when some preach Christ from rivalry?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Why would news that the gospel had reached the whole praetorian guard (v. 13) encourage believers in Philippi, a Roman colony proud of its ties to Rome?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Paul weighs living and dying in verses 21–26; what would it look like for you to say that your present life is for Christ and others?

items.text: The Humility of Christ
If there is therefore any exhortation in Christ, if any consolation of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any tender mercies and compassions,
make full my joy, that ye be of the same mind, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind;
doing nothing through faction or through vainglory, but in lowliness of mind each counting other better than himself;
not looking each of you to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
Have this mind in you, which was also in Christ Jesus:
who, existing in the form of God, counted not the being on an equality with God a thing to be grasped,
but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men;
and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, yea, the death of the cross.
Wherefore also God highly exalted him, and gave unto him the name which is above every name;
that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven and things on earth and things under the earth,
and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
Lights in the World
So then, my beloved, even as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling;
for it is God who worketh in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.
Do all things without murmurings and questionings:
that ye may become blameless and harmless, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom ye are seen as lights in the world,
holding forth the word of life; that I may have whereof to glory in the day of Christ, that I did not run in vain neither labor in vain.
Yea, and if I am offered upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I joy, and rejoice with you all:
and in the same manner do ye also joy, and rejoice with me.
Timothy and Epaphroditus
But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy shortly unto you, that I also may be of good comfort, when I know your state.
For I have no man likeminded, who will care truly for your state.
For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ.
But ye know the proof of him, that, as a child serveth a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the gospel.
Him therefore I hope to send forthwith, so soon as I shall see how it will go with me:
but I trust in the Lord that I myself also shall come shortly.
But I counted it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and fellow-worker and fellow-soldier, and your messenger and minister to my need;
since he longed after you all, and was sore troubled, because ye had heard that he was sick:
for indeed he was sick nigh unto death: but God had mercy on him; and not on him only, but on me also, that I might not have sorrow upon sorrow.
I have sent him therefore the more diligently, that, when ye see him again, ye may rejoice, and that I may be the less sorrowful.
Receive him therefore in the Lord with all joy; and hold such in honor:
because for the work of Christ he came nigh unto death, hazarding his life to supply that which was lacking in your service toward me.

summary.title: CHAPTER 2 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul appeals to them to be of one mind, doing nothing from selfishness or conceit but in humility counting others better than themselves. “Have this mind in you, which was also in Christ Jesus”: though He existed in the form of God, He emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled Himself to death on a cross. Therefore God highly exalted Him, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.

So they should work out their salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in them. They are to do all things without grumbling, shining as lights in a crooked generation. Paul hopes to send Timothy, who genuinely cares for them, and is sending back Epaphroditus, who nearly died doing the work of Christ, so they may rejoice to see him and honor such men.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: Trace the movement of Christ in verses 5–11 from equality with God to the cross to exaltation; which steps stand out most to you?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: In a city where status and honor were carefully displayed, how might the Philippians have heard Paul's call to count others better than themselves (vv. 3–4)?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Timothy and Epaphroditus are held up as examples in verses 19–30; whose quiet, costly service around you deserves to be noticed and honored?

items.text: Righteousness Through Faith in Christ
Finally, my brethren, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you, to me indeed is not irksome, but for you it is safe.
Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the concision:
for we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God, and glory in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh:
though I myself might have confidence even in the flesh: if any other man thinketh to have confidence in the flesh, I yet more:
circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee;
as touching zeal, persecuting the church; as touching the righteousness which is in the law, found blameless.
Howbeit what things were gain to me, these have I counted loss for Christ.

Yea verily, and I count all things to be loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but refuse, that I may gain Christ,
and be found in him, not having a righteousness of mine own, even that which is of the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith:
that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, becoming conformed unto his death;
if by any means I may attain unto the resurrection from the dead.
Pressing Toward the Goal
Not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect: but I press on, if so be that I may lay hold on that for which also I was laid hold on by Christ Jesus.
Brethren, I count not myself yet to have laid hold: but one thing I do, forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before,
I press on toward the goal unto the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, be thus minded: and if in anything ye are otherwise minded, this also shall God reveal unto you:
only, whereunto we have attained, by that same rule let us walk.
Brethren, be ye imitators together of me, and mark them that so walk even as ye have us for an ensample.
For many walk, of whom I told you often, and now tell you even weeping, that they are the enemies of the cross of Christ:
whose end is perdition, whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.
For our citizenship is in heaven; whence also we wait for a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:
who shall fashion anew the body of our humiliation, that it may be conformed to the body of his glory, according to the working whereby he is able even to subject all things unto himself.

summary.title: CHAPTER 3 IN SUMMARY
paras: “Rejoice in the Lord.” Paul warns against those who insist on circumcision. If anyone could trust in the flesh, Paul could: circumcised on the eighth day, of Israel, of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, a zealous persecutor, blameless under the Law. But he counts it all as loss “for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord,” to be found in Him with the righteousness that comes through faith, and to know Him and the power of His resurrection.

Paul has not yet arrived; forgetting what lies behind, he presses on toward the goal for the prize of God's upward call in Christ Jesus. He asks them to imitate him and warns, with tears, of those who live as enemies of the cross of Christ, whose god is their belly. “For our citizenship is in heaven; whence also we wait for a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ,” who will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What credentials does Paul list in verses 4–6, and why does he now count them as loss compared with knowing Christ (vv. 7–11)?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: How would the claim that our citizenship is in heaven (v. 20) have sounded to people living in a Roman colony whose citizens prized their Roman rights?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: What achievements, labels or past failures are you tempted to lean on, and what would forgetting what is behind and pressing on (vv. 13–14) mean today?

items.text: Rejoice in the Lord Always
Wherefore, my brethren beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, so stand fast in the Lord, my beloved.
I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to be of the same mind in the Lord.
Yea, I beseech thee also, true yokefellow, help these women, for they labored with me in the gospel, with Clement also, and the rest of my fellow-workers, whose names are in the book of life.
Rejoice in the Lord always: again I will say, Rejoice.
Let your forbearance be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand.
In nothing be anxious; but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honorable, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
The things which ye both learned and received and heard and saw in me, these things do: and the God of peace shall be with you.
Thanks for Their Gift
But I rejoice in the Lord greatly, that now at length ye have revived your thought for me; wherein ye did indeed take thought, but ye lacked opportunity.
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therein to be content.
I know how to be abased, and I know also how to abound: in everything and in all things have I learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in want.
I can do all things in him that strengtheneth me.
Howbeit ye did well that ye had fellowship with my affliction.
And ye yourselves also know, ye Philippians, that in the beginning of the gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church had fellowship with me in the matter of giving and receiving but ye only;
for even in Thessalonica ye sent once and again unto my need.
Not that I seek for the gift; but I seek for the fruit that increaseth to your account.
But I have all things, and abound: I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things that came from you, an odor of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, well-pleasing to God.
And my God shall supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
Now unto our God and Father be the glory for ever and ever. Amen.
Final Greetings
Salute every saint in Christ Jesus. The brethren that are with me salute you.
All the saints salute you, especially they that are of Cæsar’s household.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.

summary.title: CHAPTER 4 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul urges his beloved friends to stand firm in the Lord and pleads with Euodia and Syntyche to agree in the Lord. “Rejoice in the Lord always: again I will say, Rejoice.” Instead of being anxious, they should bring everything to God in prayer with thanksgiving, and the peace of God, which passes all understanding, will guard their hearts. They should think on whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely and of good report.

Paul rejoices that their concern for him has revived in their gift. He has learned to be content in every circumstance, in plenty and in want: “I can do all things in him that strengtheneth me.” They alone partnered with him in giving when he left Macedonia, and their gift is a fragrant offering to God, who “shall supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.” Greetings come from all the saints, “especially they that are of Caesar's household.”

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What does Paul tell the church to do with anxiety in verses 6–7, and what promise does he attach to prayer with thanksgiving?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Why might Paul publicly urge Euodia and Syntyche to agree (vv. 2–3) in a small house church where a personal quarrel could affect everyone?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Paul says he learned contentment in plenty and in want (vv. 11–13); in which circumstances of your life is contentment hardest to learn right now?

wrap.title: Philippians In Summary
paras: Philippians is a thank-you letter from prison. The church at Philippi had supported Paul from the beginning, and when they heard he was under arrest, they sent Epaphroditus with a gift. Paul writes back with warmth and affection, and the letter rings with joy, even though he is chained to a soldier and waiting to learn whether he will live or die.

Paul's joy comes from his focus on Christ: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” His chains have spread the gospel through the Praetorian Guard and made other believers bold. Whatever happens, he can be content, because he can do all things through Christ who strengthens him. At the heart of the letter is the great passage about Christ's humility (2:5–11). Though He was in the form of God, He emptied Himself, became a servant and died on a cross, and God exalted Him above every name. Paul holds this out as the pattern for a church troubled by rivalry and disagreement: humility, unity and looking to others' interests.

Paul also warns against trusting in religious credentials. He gave up all his own advantages to know Christ and to be found in Him, with a righteousness that comes through faith. He presses on toward the goal, and he reminds this proud Roman colony that their true citizenship is in heaven, where their Savior is.

The letter closes with practical encouragement: rejoice always, pray instead of worrying, think on what is good, and trust God to supply every need. The message in one line: joy and peace are found not in circumstances but in Christ, whose humility shows us how to live together and whose power sustains us in every situation.
